domestic.debt_note: Re-checked this cycle: federal government debt rose to ~Rs82tn by end-May 2026 (https://tribune.com.pk/story/2616882/govt-debt-rises-to-rs82tr), but the debt-to-GDP ratio has been on a declining path, cited at ~68.5% for FY25-26 vs 75% in FY22-23 per the same report -- a different (lower) figure than the 70.7% end-FY25 figure carried in prior cycles, likely reflecting a later-vintage estimate/rebasing, flagged as a discrepancy rather than reconciled. Separately, the government has retired a record Rs4.722tn (~$17bn) of public debt ahead of maturity, extending average maturity from 2.7yrs (FY24) to 3.8yrs (FY26) (https://propakistani.pk/2026/07/14/pakistan-clears-record-rs-4-7-trillion-debt-before-maturity/); the government also raised Rs2.068tn in a fresh MTB auction this week with all-tenor cutoffs still below the 11.5% policy rate: 1M 11.3968%, 3M/6M eased similarly (https://propakistani.pk/2026/07/08/govt-borrows-rs-2-trillion-from-local-debt-market/); a first-ever dollar-settled, rupee-linked bond and fresh Eurobond/Sukuk issuance are being prepped for FY27 market borrowing (https://propakistani.pk/2026/07/08/pakistan-to-launch-first-ever-dollar-settled-rupee-bonds/).
domestic.remittances: Unchanged, re-confirmed this cycle: FY26 remittances hit an all-time record $41.6bn, +8.6% YoY vs $38.3bn in FY25, meeting the government's $41-42bn estimate; GCC (Saudi Arabia, UAE) supplies well over half of inflows (https://www.geo.tv/latest/672412-psx-gains-nearly-1-as-oil-eases-reserves-rise, https://www.thenews.pk/story/1424957-fy26-remittances-hit-416bn-showing-86-yearly-growth). The GCC-heavy sourcing remains a forward risk channel if the live Hormuz standoff disrupts Gulf labour markets/freight, not yet visible in the data.
domestic.current_account: No new official current-account print located this cycle; the last hard cumulative figure remains the 11-month Jul-May FY26 surplus of ~$255mn vs a $1.62bn deficit a year earlier, with SBP guiding the full FY26 current account to close 'slightly in surplus' for a second straight year (https://www.brecorder.com/news/40429111, https://www.dawn.com/news/2008684). That guidance predates the live Hormuz standoff; since over 80% of Pakistan's crude imports transit the strait, the naval blockade (still in effect, though the proposed 20% cargo toll was rescinded on 2026-07-14) remains a forward FY27-Q1 import-bill risk not yet captured in any print.

REGIME CALL: neutral, upgraded from risk-off. Rationale -- (1) the acute leg of the Hormuz shock is de-escalating: Trump rescinded the cargo toll within 24 hours of announcing it, Brent has pulled back from its $86.57 multi-week peak to $85.03, and VIX eased -2.18% rather than spiking further; (2) PSX's own tape confirms the relief -- today's +1.02% rebound followed two brutal down sessions, showing the market pricing in reduced near-term escalation risk, not a broad global risk-off (S&P/Dow both flat-to-up); (3) desk georisk score eased to 55/100 moderate from 59, though conflict stress remains maxed, so this is a genuine but incomplete de-escalation, not an all-clear; (4) domestic anchors remain solidly constructive and unchanged: SBP on hold, CPI easing, IMF program on track, reserves stable and growing, record remittances, sub-policy-rate T-bill yields, aggressive early debt retirement. Net: neither a clean risk-on (the naval blockade is still active, Iran still contesting the strait, and no new current-account/reserves print yet captures any of this week's oil spike) nor a risk-off requiring maximum defensiveness. Regime moves to neutral -- normal setup limits apply, but energy-cost-sensitive import sectors still warrant caution pending confirmation the blockade stands down.

favored: E&P (upstream oil & gas -- direct beneficiary of any residual elevated realized crude/gas prices)
banks (quality/defensive, high-rate carry, sub-policy-rate T-bill funding costs supportive of margins)
fertilizer (domestic-demand defensive, low direct oil-import beta)
avoid: OMCs (inventory/margin and circular-debt risk from volatile, weekly-repriced fuel costs while the blockade's resolution is still unconfirmed)
autos (imported-input cost + weaker consumer demand under fuel/inflation pressure)
textiles/exporters (Gulf freight-cost exposure while the naval blockade remains formally in effect)
